title: When the Ledger Burns
premise: In 1859, on a storm-battered Irish coast, widowed lighthouse keeper Mirabel Kavanagh receives a sealed letter from her late husband's estranged uncle naming the Kavanagh family in the smuggling and wrecking conspiracy that has quietly enriched the local gentry for decades. As the great storms of that winter isolate the coast, Mirabel discovers her husband's death five years ago was no accident, and that the ledger recording every paid-off official is hidden in the lighthouse itself. Racing against the victors' hired historians who will burn the record clean, she must decide whether exposing the truth will save or destroy the community that depends on its silence. In the end, she copies the ledger page by page, hides the originals where only fire can reach them, and testifies at the assizes — winning justice for the drowned, but losing the lighthouse, her name, and nearly her life.
about_author: Freya Halloran is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing maritime court records along the Atlantic seaboard. She writes historical fiction about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Light That Keeps Its Own Hours
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A winter storm forces her to keep the lamp burning alone through the night, establishing her competence, isolation, and the ritual silences of the light station. She finds her late husband Tomas's old logbook with pages cut out. Emotional beat: grief worn smooth into routine, but a first crack of unease.

chapters.title: A Letter Sealed Twice
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A solicitor's clerk arrives through the storm with a sealed letter from Uncle Declan Kavanagh, posted before his death, naming the family in 'the wrecking business' and warning that 'the historians are already bought.' She burns it instinctively — then regrets it. Beat: fear overriding curiosity, and the cost of learned silence.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brings Back
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. After the storm, wreckage washes ashore including a ship's manifest dated the night of a famous wrecking twenty years prior — the same night her husband's father grew rich. The harbor master, Ollie Brennan, watches her too closely as she pockets it. Beat: the past surfacing literally, and the sense of being watched.

chapters.title: The Gentry's Gratitude
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Squire Ambrose Fennelly invites her to the big house, all charm and veiled warnings, offering to fund the lighthouse's repairs if she keeps her lamp pointed seaward and her questions landward. She accepts, hating herself. Beat: seduction of complicity; power dressed as generosity.

chapters.title: Tomas's Cut Pages
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, with flashback. Reconstructing the missing logbook pages from memory and tide tables, she realizes Tomas logged a false light the night of his own drowning — someone else was keeping the true one. Beat: the marriage she thought she knew reassembling into something stranger and braver.

chapters.title: The Historian Arrives
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A polished gentleman, Mr. Quill, arrives 'to write the definitive history of the coast,' interviewing families and buying papers by the pound. He interviews Mirabel last, longest, and most gently. Beat: menace in courtesy; she understands the letter's warning — the record itself is the battlefield.

chapters.title: Declan's Daughter
chapters.summary: Nora Kavanagh's POV (introduced). Declan's estranged daughter comes down from Dublin, half-convinced her father died mad. She and Mirabel circle each other with suspicion, then trade what each knows: Nora has the letter's second copy; Mirabel has the manifest. Beat: alliance forming out of mutual distrust.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Drowned
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Following Tomas's tide-table cipher, she finds a hidden compartment beneath the lamp room containing the ledger — decades of payments for darkened lights and false signals, signed by Fennelly's father and grandfather. Beat: awe curdling into horror; inheritance revealed as poison.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: Nora's POV. The two women decode the ledger: nine local families implicated, including the priest who buried the wrecked sailors and the doctor who certified their drownings accidental. Nora wants it published immediately; Mirabel argues they need living witnesses first. Beat: strategy versus rage; the sisters-in-law become co-conspirators.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Reads
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Quill begins courting the town's memory, rewriting the wrecking as tragic weather. Villagers who once greeted Mirabel now cross the street. Her housekeeper resigns in tears, begging her to stop asking questions. Beat: social isolation tightening; the price of truth made personal.

chapters.title: Fire on the Headland
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The lighthouse's oil store catches fire in suspicious circumstances; she fights it alone through the night and saves the tower but loses the boathouse — and realizes the ledger was the target, saved only because she'd moved it. Beat: escalation from pressure to violence; resolve hardening.

chapters.title: Ollie Brennan's Confession
chapters.summary: Ollie's POV. The aging harbor master, dying and frightened, comes to the light station at dawn: he was the boy who rowed the false signals, and Tomas discovered it. He gives Mirabel Tomas's final letter, which he'd been paid to intercept and never delivered. Beat: guilt finding its voice; the past asking forgiveness.

chapters.title: Tomas's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Reading Tomas's words — he meant to testify, and named the man who killed him — Mirabel grieves properly for the first time in five years. She decides: not revenge, but the record. She begins copying the ledger by hand, page by page, every night after the lamp is lit. Beat: grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Quill Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Quill reveals he knows what she has, and offers not threats but partnership: let him shape the story, soften the nine names, and the Kavanaghs emerge sympathetic. He shows her the commissioned draft already praising the Fennellys. Beat: the seduction of a clean, survivable lie — her darkest temptation.

chapters.title: The Assizes Open
chapters.summary: Nora's POV. Spring assizes begin in the county town; a reformist judge has summoned witnesses after an anonymous package (sent by Nora) reached Dublin. The nine families close ranks; Fennelly's counsel paints Declan as a madman and Mirabel as a grieving woman manipulated. Beat: hope and danger arriving together.

chapters.title: Witness for the Weather
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. On the stand, opposing counsel dismantles her credibility piece by piece until she abandons the ledger argument and does something unplanned: she reads Tomas's last letter aloud, entire, letting his voice do what hers could not. Beat: vulnerability as weapon; the courtroom silenced.

chapters.title: The Ninth Name Speaks
chapters.summary: Father Colm's POV. The elderly priest, cornered by the ledger and his own dying conscience, takes the stand and confirms everything — payments, burials, the order to stay silent. The case cracks open. Beat: the corrupt institution turning witness; catharsis with a bitter taste.

chapters.title: Fennelly's Last Storm
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Facing ruin, Fennelly comes to the lighthouse at night — first to buy the ledger, then, refused, to take it. In the struggle on the gallery, he falls; Mirabel saves him with the breeches buoy rigging, refusing to become his kind of keeper. He confesses before the arriving constables. Beat: climax; moral victory over vengeance.

chapters.title: What the Victors' Historians Missed
chapters.summary: Nora's POV. Verdicts fall; estates are seized; Quill's commissioned history is pulped when the original ledger surfaces in evidence. But Nora discovers Quill kept a second, subtler manuscript — and chooses, like Mirabel once did, whether to burn or to bear witness. Beat: the theme made explicit; memory as choice.

chapters.title: The Ledger Burns
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. With her hand-copied duplicate deposited with the court and printed, Mirabel burns the original in the lamp room, freeing the town from the object everyone would kill for. The truth survives; the weapon doesn't. Beat: release; inheritance transformed from burden to gift.

chapters.title: A New Keeper's Log
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The Crown appoints a new keeper; Mirabel, her name cleared but her post dissolved, prepares to leave. The town that shunned her lines the quay in silence — then, one by one, brings small gifts: bread, rope, a repaired clock. Beat: quiet restoration; belonging earned rather than inherited.

chapters.title: Which Silences Keep People Safe
chapters.summary: Mirabel's and Nora's alternating final entries. On the coach out, Mirabel writes the opening line of her own account — this book — deciding some silences protect and others bury, and hers will be spoken. Final image: the lighthouse beam sweeping behind them, steady, keeping its hours without her. Beat: peace; memory entrusted forward.
